item.title: Pompey boss apologises to Cardiff players over fan incident
item.description: Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho apologises to Cardiff City players after an incident involving home fans at Fratton Park during their Championship match.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho has apologised to Cardiff City players after an incident involving home fans at Fratton Park.

In the 72nd minute of Portsmouth's 2-0 Championship win over the Bluebirds, Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik got into a physical altercation with a fan as he went to retrieve a ball.

Cardiff head coach Brian Barry-Murphy claimed afterwards that Bielik "got slapped in the face", while clips circulating on social media appeared to show the Poland international grabbing a young fan around his upper body.

In the aftermath, another fan threw a ball at the head of Cardiff defender Perry Ng, which resulted in both fans being ejected from the stadium.

Speaking after the match, Pompey boss Mousinho said: "The referee said that, as Krystian went to get the ball, there was a little bit of a kerfuffle and one of the supporters struck him.

"It wasn't a good incident. I have just seen him there, and he was OK, but that's not the point, we can't be having that.

"We want to create a really difficult atmosphere at Fratton Park, we have done that successfully over the past few years.

"Sometimes it tips over, I understand that, I don't think it needs to tip over to that extent.

"We extend our apologies to the players, Cardiff and make sure we can try to cut it out."

Cardiff boss Barry-Murphy described the incident as "not acceptable", but applauded the officials for their handling of the situation.

"Krystian went to get the ball back from the stands and got slapped in the face," said Barry-Murphy.

"I just wanted to make sure he was protected and make sure he was OK. He is.

"I thought the referee and his staff handled the incident impeccably.

"I think the players are always subjected to different things, it's not acceptable what happens.

"They don't expect that sort of treatment. My job is to protect the players but really my focus is on trying to make sure that we play well and win.

"So I'm sure the club and the FA (Football Association) will look at this and implement the correct process."

item.title: South Africa finish strongly to take 2-1 series lead against All Blacks
item.description: South Africa eventually overpower a spirited New Zealand as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 series lead.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Greatest Rivalry Series - third Test

South Africa (12) 29

Tries: Arendse, penalty try, Kriel, Marx Cons: Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Mngomezulu

New Zealand (12) 24

Tries: Savea 2, Jordan, Taukei'aho Cons: Love, McKenzie

South Africa eventually overpowered a spirited New Zealand, who could only outrun their hosts' set-piece power for so long, as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 lead in a high-quality 'Greatest Rivalry' series.

The two sides traded two tries each in a tight first half, with New Zealand's composure and ambition with ball in hand stretching South Africa's onrushing defence.

The All Blacks sniffed a famous victory when Will Jordan chased after his own kick ahead and crossed for a 17-12 lead in the 55th minute.

But Jesse Kriel barged through Leroy Carter to cross at the other end shortly after and, reprieved, South Africa took full advantage.

Malcolm Marx plunged over at the back of juggernaut maul and a Sacha Feinberg Mngomezulu penalty gave South Africa a cushion that Samisoni Taukei'aho's final-play try could dent, but not fully deflate.

The two teams will meet in a fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore next weekend, with New Zealand, who won the opening match, looking to snatch a draw in the series.

More to follow.

item.title: Alpine's Gasly beats Russell to stunning Monza pole
item.description: Alpine driver Pierre Gasly takes a stunning pole position at the Italian Grand Prix, ahead of Mercedes' George Russell.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Alpine driver Pierre Gasly took a stunning pole position at the Italian Grand Prix.

The Frenchman, who took his sole Formula 1 victory at this race for Red Bull's junior team in 2020, beat Mercedes' George Russell by 0.060 seconds.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was third with the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton fourth and fifth despite an upgraded engine.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen took sixth, and McLaren's Lando Norris only ninth after a messy session for the world champion.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes qualified seventh but will start at the back because of a grid penalty for taking a new engine.

More to follow

item.title: New season, same flaw - Chelsea title hopes already under scrutiny
item.description: With 11 minutes remaining, Chelsea appeared to be cruising to victory in their WSL opener against Aston Villa. So how did they throw it away?
item.content:encoded:
• Published

With 11 minutes remaining, Chelsea appeared to be cruising to victory in their Women's Super League opener against Aston Villa.

Yet, after 57 touches in the opposition box, 23 shots inside the area, hitting the crossbar and having another goal disallowed for offside, somehow they drew 1-1.

The statistics are alarming given they did everything right to win, except score more.

It is an issue that has reared its head on several occasions during manager Sonia Bompastor's time in charge and is why many have tipped rivals Arsenal to win the title this season.

While England international Lauren James oozed quality and summer signing Katie McCabe had a strong WSL debut, Chelsea's lack of ruthlessness in front of goal could prove costly.

"We started really well. We wanted to start with energy and create opportunities but at this level, we need to be more clinical," McCabe, who joined Chelsea from Arsenal this summer, told BBC Sport.

"We're frustrated to drop points at home. We're not going to panic - it's the start of the season. We'll look to rectify next week.

"But we're disappointed. It's not Chelsea standards to drop points at home."

Limited attacking options cost Chelsea

Chelsea attempted 34 shots in the game, their highest total in a WSL match since the start of last season.

James hit the ground running with a superb strike that flew into the roof of the net within 11 minutes and Chelsea fans expected the floodgates to open.

Villa barely laid a glove on their opponents and had only five touches in Chelsea's box.

But, against the run of play, Noelle Maritz's shot ricocheted off goalkeeper Hannah Hampton and bounced in off Chelsea defender Veerle Buurman late on.

Villa boss Natalia Arroyo threw her arms in the air and their supporters punctured the silence of disbelief that fell across Stamford Bridge.

"If you analyse the performance and the statistics, then you would say it's crazy that we didn't win. We created so many opportunities," said Bompastor.

"The reality of football is that if we were two or three nil up then the game is over. It's a completely different game in the second half.

"We have to speed up the game, keep that momentum and sustain that. We need to make sure we accelerate to kill the game. That is not what happened today.

"At the end, we are all frustrated because it's not a good result."

Bompastor's biggest frustration was that she could do little to help.

With summer signing Melvine Malard out with a minor injury picked up in training and Mayra Ramirez still continuing her recovery, attacking options were limited.

England forward Aggie Beever-Jones led the line, taking the baton from recently-departed Sam Kerr, but her confidence is clearly low.

She had opportunities but scuppered them and when she did eventually put the ball in the net, it was ruled out for offside.

"What can we do in this scenario? We have to stay confident, stick together and work hard," said manager Bompastor.

"In football some of these things are mental. It's the mentality - the mindset of being ruthless and clinical in the box.

"The best teams don't need many opportunities. They just need one or two and maybe that's enough to win the game. That is something we need to work on."

A dent in Chelsea's title credentials?

This was not the first time Chelsea have dropped points because of a lack of ruthlessness.

Despite beginning the 25-26 WSL campaign with victory over eventual champions Manchester City, they ended up finishing third.

Four draws proved costly, on top of three defeats - one particular loss at Everton in December ending a 585-day unbeaten streak in the WSL.

In that 1-0 defeat, Chelsea had 79% possession, 30 shots and hit the woodwork three times. It was deja vu against Aston Villa on Saturday.

"You should be able to convert those chances. In the first half, they had chance after chance," said former England striker Ellen White on BBC One.

"To go for the title you have to score and get points on the board. This is two points dropped. Last season, they only dropped six points at home."

Manchester City begin their title defence on Sunday at home to newly-promoted Birmingham City (14:30 BST), while Arsenal travel to Brighton (12:00 BST).

That will give Chelsea a better idea of their competition after London City Lionesses put down a marker with a win at home to Manchester United on Friday night.

Bompastor hopes the return of other attacking players will improve their conversion rate going forward.

But the biggest issue is the hardest one to find a solution for at Chelsea.

"Some things are easier to coach and other things are more difficult. The mindset you can improve, but you have to have a killer instinct and desire inside," she added.

"We need to stay together and a lot of this is keeping the confidence. We just need to analyse all these things to help the players be confident for the next game."

item.title: Modric plans to play for Croatia past 41st birthday
item.description: Luke Modric, 41, is not ready to retire from international football and hopes to play for Croatia in upcoming Nations League games, including against England.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Luka Modric turns 41 on Wednesday but is not ready to retire from international football just yet.

The Croatia FA has announced, external that their captain intends to continue playing for the national team in upcoming Nations League games, including against England.

His decision coincides with the return of Slaven Bilic as manager, with the former West Ham boss helping to guide Modric's fledgling international career in his first stint in charge of the Croatia side, between 2006 and 2012.

Modric earned his first senior cap in March 2006, just before Bilic was named Croatia manager for the first time, and has since gone on to make 202 appearances for his country.

He was expected to call it a day after this summer's World Cup, when Zlatko Dalic's side were knocked out in the last 32 by Portugal.

"Of course, Luka's decision makes me extremely happy," said Bilic, who was manager of Croatia when they denied Steve McLaren's England side qualification for the 2008 Euros.

"We are all aware what he brings to Croatia, both on and off the pitch.

"I'm looking forward to working with him again, after 14 years, and we both share a strong ambition to keep Croatia a top, successful team, shoulder to shoulder with the best teams in the world."

Modric, who currently plays for AC Milan, won the Golden Ball at the 2018 World Cup in Russia, when he helped Croatia reach the final, where they lost to France.

He was also part of the side that finished third in Qatar, four years later.

After playing his part in McLaren's "wally with the brolly" moment at Wembley in the 2008 Euro qualifiers, Modric helped Croatia reach the quarter-finals in Austria and Switzerland.

Croatia's next internationals are in the in the Nations League - away to Czech Republic on 26 September and Spain on 29 September.

They then host England in the competition on 3 October, with the return fixture at Wembley on 12 November.

item.title: Scott shines, Dedic struggles - Newcastle v Bournemouth player ratings
item.description: How Newcastle United and Bournemouth's players rated in their Premier League match.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Substitute Jacob Ramsey scored a late equaliser as Newcastle United came from behind to draw 2-2 against Bournemouth at St James' Park.

Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below.

Newcastle United

Lukas Hornicek: A little unfortunate for the second goal in particular after the ball came back off the upright and bounced off him. One or two moments of miscommunication at the back. 5

Amar Dedic: Made an impressive start to his Newcastle career, and carries a real threat going forward, but caught out defensively for both goals. Did swing in the ball for the equaliser, though. 4

Malick Thiaw: Stand-in captain in Dan Burn's absence once again, but could only watch on as he put through the net after his block on Alex Scott's cross looped into the bottom corner. 5

Sven Botman: A poor clearance before Marcus Tavernier's opener but went on to make a couple of crucial interventions to deny Evanilson. 5

Lewis Hall: Substituted at half-time in the corresponding fixture back in April but coped better with Rayan this time. 6

Nico Gonzalez: Struggled to have the same effect as his impressive debut against Tottenham Hotspur. Missed a tackle on Tavernier before Bournemouth's second goal and only partially blocked Scott's effort in the build-up to the visitors' first. 5

Lewis Miley: So much potential, and still so young at 20, but struggled to get a handle on Bournemouth's midfield. Passing not to usual standard. 5

Anthony Elanga: Quickly frustrated with refereeing decisions going against him. Got little change from Adrien Truffert. 5

Joe Willock: Couldn't fault his effort as he chased down Bournemouth players and attempted to make blocks. Came close to equalising with a header. 5

Harvey Barnes: Stepped up when Newcastle were on very shaky ground with a stunning goal from the hosts' first shot on target. Often frustrated by failure, but always capable of a big moment. 7

Yoane Wissa: Looks better in the number 10 role in this system than up top. Repeatedly dropped deep to get involved. Showed determination to dig out a cross for a big Willock chance. 5

Subs:

Matias Fernandez-Pardo (on 63, Willock): Got a huge welcome on his debut. Quickly won a free-kick and worked hard to win the ball back. 6

Jacob Ramsey: Popped up with a precious equaliser to secure a point with a well-taken finish. 7

Jacob Murphy (on 77, Elanga): 6

Sean Steur (on 77, Gonzalez): 6

Livramento (on 90, Hall)

Subs not used: Nick Pope, Fabian Schar, Aladji Bamba, Bazoumana Toure

Bournemouth

Djordje Petrovic: Little he could do for Barnes' goal, but otherwise a relatively comfortable afternoon. 6

Adam Smith: Played a role in Tavernier's opener by nudging the ball to Scott in the build-up. Tested on one or two moments defensively, but still showing his value at 35. 6

James Hill: Solid. Has already become a very important player for manager Marco Rose. 6

Antonio Silva: Took a nasty blow to the head from Elanga's shoulder, but the summer signing shook it off. 6

Adrien Truffert: Coped expertly with the in-form Elanga and caused Dedic real problems going the other way. 7

Tyler Adams: First competitive start under Rose. Could have got closer to Barnes for Newcastle's goal, but hard to see him coming out of the side after this display. 7

Alex Scott: So influential. Played a key role in both of his side's goals. Passing and vision stood out throughout. 8

Rayan: Not as effective as he was in the corresponding fixture last season. Rose was roaring at him at one stage. 5

Marcus Tavernier: Showed great anticipation to put the visitors in front. He's now scored in each of his past three trips to St James' Park. Could have netted a couple on this visit. 7

Justin Kluivert: Helped set up Bournemouth's crucial second goal after boldly letting fly from 35 yards out. Always a handful. 7

Evanilson: Had a real battle with Botman. Missed a couple of decent chances but worked hard throughout. 6

item.title: Pogacar will miss rest of season after Vuelta crash
item.description: Five-time Tour de France champion Tadej Pogacar will not race again this season after suffering injuries including a fracture in his neck at the Vuelta a Espana.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Five-time Tour de France champion Tadej Pogacar will not race again this season after suffering injuries including a neck fracture at the Vuelta a Espana.

The injury, which he suffered last month on the race's eighth stage, means the Slovenian will miss out on the chance to defend his title at the upcoming World Championships.

He crashed out of the Vuelta from a dominant position as race leader and required surgery on a broken collarbone, suffered a concussion, a "stable" fracture in his neck and multiple abrasions.

The 27-year-old, who was aiming to complete the set of Grand Tour titles, adding the Vuelta to his single Giro d'Italia victory and Tour de France wins, was due to defend his rainbow jersey at the World Championships in Montreal later this month.

"Of course, this isn't the way I wanted my season to finish," Pogacar said in a statement released by his team, UAE Team Emirates-XRG.

"Right now, the most important thing is to recover properly and give my body the time it needs.

"It has been a season with many special moments and I'm proud of what we achieved together. Now I'll focus on getting healthy, supporting the guys from home, and coming back next year ready for what's ahead."

In October, Pogacar was due to defend his title at the European Championships in Ljubljana, in his home country, and in the Il Lombardia - the final one-day Monument race of the season.

The team said that the decision not to race again until 2027 would allow him to return to full health "without placing a timeline on his return to competition".

UAE Team Emirates-XRG also announced their leading rider had agreed to extend his contract by two years, until 2032.

item.title: Hughes steps down as Liverpool sporting director
item.description: Richard Hughes steps down from his position as sporting director of Liverpool and is set to join Saudi side Al Hilal.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Liverpool sporting director Richard Hughes has stepped down and is set to join Saudi side Al Hilal.

Hughes had only been at the club since June 2024, after moving from a similar position at Bournemouth, and his exit had been expected with his contract set to expire in June 2027.

In the summer he oversaw a transfer spend of about £200m, including the signing of Bradley Barcola from Paris St-Germain.

"I'll always follow and support the club with great affection, and I wish everyone involved nothing but success for this season and beyond," said Hughes, in a statement released by Liverpool.

Hughes, 47, arrived at Anfield after the departure of long-time manager Jurgen Klopp and was instrumental in the appointment of his successor, Arne Slot, who led Liverpool to a 20th Premier League title in his first season as manager.

Hughes oversaw the £125m record signing of Alexander Isak last summer and the £116m arrival of Florian Wirtz.

But Slot was unable to match his initial success and Liverpool finished fifth last season, prompting the Dutch manager's departure and his replacement by Andoni Iraola, who Hughes worked with at Bournemouth.

Mike Gordon, president of the Fenway Sports Group which owns Liverpool, said: "Richard joined us at the start of a period of change, embracing that responsibility by leading our football operations department and overseeing recruitment while also providing valuable support to our coaching staff.

"The results we achieved in these areas during this period are testament to this contribution. Nevertheless, we respect Richard's life choices and wish him and his family well in their next venture."

item.title: Clarke gave SFA 'a little shove' over new contract
item.description: Steve Clarke says he had to cajole the Scottish FA into handing him a new contract as national head coach shortly before the World Cup finals this summer because he felt the governing body was hedging its bets.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Former Scotland boss Steve Clarke says he had to cajole the Scottish FA into handing him a new contract as national head coach shortly before the World Cup finals this summer because he felt the governing body was hedging its bets.

But the 63-year-old insists he nevertheless always planned to resign if he failed to lead Scotland beyond the group stage for the first time.

Speaking for the first time since the tournament in the Americas, Clarke was being interviewed by former Chelsea and Scotland team-mate Pat Nevin at Spartans Community Foundation dinner in Edinburgh.

Asked about his exit from the job despite the four-year contract he signed on the eve of the tournament, and quoted by The Scotsman, he said: "It was never really a change of mind.

"I am quite a complex person. I wanted to control my narrative."

Clark added: "Obviously we got to March and I hadn't been offered a new contract, which I thought was pretty strange. You start to think are they hedging their bets a little bit, waiting on the tournament in the summer.

"So I did a little bit in the media in March to give the SFA a little shove. We negotiated non-stop from the beginning of April really to the middle of May, just before the Curacao game.

"And I said to them if we don't agree a new contract before we go to the World Cup then I will say I am leaving the job. They panicked a little bit and gave me the new contract.

"It was like drawing teeth trying to get it over the line. But we got it over the line anyway.

"But I always knew in my head that if we did not get out of the group stage then I would probably leave. The only way I would have stayed on is if they had been three fantastic games and they went against you."

Scotland beat Haiti 1-0 but lost by the same score to Morocco before a 3-0 loss to Brazil left them waiting for an unlikely series of results to allow them to progress as one of the better third-place sides.

"We had to stay for four or five days [in Charlotte], the longest four or five days ever just sitting and waiting, knowing you are going home because the goal difference was not good enough," he recalled.

"I knew we needed four points. I got hammered in the media for saying that. Somebody hammered me for saying, 'nah, that's us, we are going home'. But I was right."

Clarke revealed he spoke to several senior players following the Brazil game and sensed that they needed to hear a different voice if they are to make history by reaching the knockout stage at Euro 2028.

Meantime, he spoke to new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli last week to wish him well and believes "even Scotland" cannot fail to qualify given two spots in the finals will be reserved for the best-ranked host who have not qualified as a group winner or runner-up.

item.title: FIA appeal court refutes Briatore impartiality claim
item.description: The FIA court of appeal refutes a claim by Alpine boss Flavio Briatore which it says "question the independence and impartiality of the judges".
item.content:encoded:
• Published

The FIA court of appeal has refuted a claim by Alpine boss Flavio Briatore which it says "questions the independence and impartiality of the judges" in a case brought by McLaren and Red Bull against the French team.

Briatore claimed on Friday that one of the court of appeal judges in the case that ended with the court re-instating a penalty on Alpine's Pierre Gasly in the Monaco Grand Prix had "links" with McLaren.

The statement by the highest legal authority of motorsport's governing body said that court of appeal judges are "subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA judicial and disciplinary rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA compliance officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved".

It added that the parties to the dispute were invited both before and after the hearing "to raise any issues concerning the proceedings or the composition of the court. None did so".

It added: "No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.

"A court's decision can leave room for various interpretations and comments as for its legal merits; that is fair and accepted by all the judges.

"The court is confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges.

"The FIA courts remain committed to the independence and impartiality of their judges and to the integrity of the judicial process."

The FIA says the court of appeal "operates independently" of the wider organisation.

On Friday Briatore had said: "One of the judges act like a prosecutor. This is not a big problem. The problem is he's very linked with the McLaren company."

The 76-year-old Italian's claims were based on a charity auction held in California in 2018 which the judge in question had attended and to which he claimed "McLaren gave two, three McLaren cars".

"This was quite unfair," Briatore said. "One of the judges was linked with a team that was protesting us."

Asked why Alpine had not raised objections at the hearing, Briatore said: "We found out, after the meeting, logically, not before, we found out this guy was linked with the McLaren team. This is what I think."

The case against the decision to drop two pit-lane speeding penalties on Gasly in Monaco was brought by both McLaren and Red Bull.

The court of appeal decision demoted Gasly back to seventh place, and promoted three Red Bull drivers and one McLaren driver higher in the points.

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was put back into third place, McLaren's Oscar Piastri to fourth and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad to fifth and sixth.

Briatore made no reference to Red Bull in his comments.

McLaren have responded angrily to Briatore's comments.

Privately, they reject them out of hand and are angry that what they believe are unfounded claims have been given a public airing in a news conference.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella attended the same news conference in which Briatore made his remarks.

Stella said: "I find that this conference going in this direction is quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect.

"And if anybody makes these kind of allegations - which seem quite serious - they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

"The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal, was conducted to the highest standards and we should not question this phase as has been done."

item.title: No Brits left in US Open singles - but are there reasons to be positive?
item.description: There will be no British interest in the second week of another Grand Slam at the US Open - but is it all doom and gloom?
item.content:encoded:
• Published

For the fourth time in five majors, there will be no British interest in the second week when the US Open moves into the latter stages.

Underwhelming performances at this year's Australian Open, French Open and Wimbledon led to a series of inquests into what was going wrong.

But there is not quite the same sense of doom and gloom, despite everyone being wiped out after the second round in New York.

"Do I think there could be an inquest? I always think there's things that British tennis could do better. So yes, definitely," said British women's number three Francesca Jones.

"Do I think it's something that's concerning? No, not at all.

"The level is getting better and everyone is dangerous on their day."

With the Grand Slam season now over for the singles players, BBC Sport analyses the positives and negatives in British tennis.

Another Slam semi-final and more top 100 players - the positives

Arthur Fery's extraordinary run to the Wimbledon semi-finals is the clear highlight.

The 24-year-old was ranked 114th in the world and needed a wildcard to play at the All England Club, but took full advantage to produce a performance which nobody could have predicted.

Fery was the only player to reach the second week at a Slam this year and has been heralded by British tennis bosses as proof their talent development pathway is working.

Nine Britons competing in the US Open main-draw singles - the most since 1981- is also highlighted as a sign of recent improvement.

That figure does not include 2021 US Open champion Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper, who both missed out with long-term injuries.

"We obviously want more and more competitors in the second week of Slams - just like the British public," said LTA chief executive Scott Lloyd.

"But the fact we've had four different British players make Grand Slam semi-finals since 2021 - you have to go back 30 years before Andy Murray to have four - shows there is no question that the direction of travel has improved.

"We've just got to keep driving for more - and that's what we're trying to do day in and day out."

Five British men are set to feature in the world top 100 after the US Open, with Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski, Toby Samuel and Jacob Fearnley representing the highest tally since February 2024.

On the women's side, there will be two players - Katie Boulter and Raducanu - in the top 100, although Jones and Harriet Dart moved back to the cusp after reaching the Flushing Meadows second round.

"We've sent 12 players to the world's top 100 over the past eight years and four of those have played Grand Slam semi-finals," said LTA performance director Michael Bourne.

"I'm not sure what other period in the modern era where we've had that level of productivity. Hopefully the number in the top 100 will rise over the next year."

Injuries, trailing other nations and coaching issues - the negatives

Despite those figures, some will argue that Britain - with its rich tradition and spending power as a Grand Slam nation - is still punching well below its weight.

A glut of injuries for many British players over the past year has not helped the cause.

Former world number four Draper has barely played over the past year because of an arm injury, while Sonay Kartal - who cracked the top 50 last year - has also dropped outside of the top 100 following a long-term back issue.

Britain has fewer players inside the top 100 than the United States, Australia and France, who also benefit from the revenue generated by hosting Grand Slam tournaments.

It also trails nations such as Spain, Italy, the Czech Republic and Argentina, who are all heralded for their talent production.

But Britain cannot simply "pick up a plan" of what others are doing as every country has its own "tennis ecosystem", says Bourne.

Lloyd adds: "We're competing in one of the most internationally elite sports out there and the landscape is vastly different to 40 or 50 years ago in terms of the number of countries which have representation at the top.

"We're ambitious, we want to drive for more, but we honestly believe the indicators are positive. We're moving in the right direction and stronger than where we have been historically."

Encouraging more British children to pick up a racquet from an early age is crucial to developing the next generation of stars.

Draper, Raducanu and Fery - who entered the LTA system at a young age - provide the blueprint.

There are 4.3m juniors playing tennis annually with 1.9m playing every month, which Lloyd says are both all-time records.

But there is a concern that a lack of high-level coaching is stunting the development of many more promising talents.

Bourne admits the UK needs a "higher base" of coaches, adding that one of the LTA's key strategies is "spending time and effort" on developing them.

Chris Marshall, a senior performance coach with over 25 years' experience, fears many youngsters are being priced out of tennis because parents cannot afford quality coaching.

"To fund a 12-year-old at county level right now requires anywhere from £500 to £1,000 a month for coaching, travel, and tournament fees," Marshall, who founded the Young Champs programme to provide free and discounted coaching for children, told BBC Sport.

"It is a massive, stressful financial barrier that makes the sport a non-starter for the vast majority of British families.

"We can't sit around lamenting the lack of British interest in the second week when we are restricting the pipeline that feeds it."

item.title: Eyes on big prize as Swansea and Wrexham collide
item.description: Swansea City and Wrexham meet in a mouthwatering Welsh derby with stakes high as both clubs eye the Premier League.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Swansea City and Wrexham will meet in the league for the 33rd time this Saturday evening.

Rarely, if ever, can there have been a more eagerly anticipated encounter between two clubs who are rivals, of sorts, despite being from opposite corners of Wales.

The fixture which matters most to Swansea fans is against Cardiff City, their neighbours in the south of the country.

For Wrexham, meanwhile, local squabbles with Chester and Shrewsbury Town have traditionally been the games which have come with the greatest significance.

But Swansea against Wrexham has a derby feel too, even though the cities are more than 100 miles apart.

And this particular meeting comes with increased stakes because both clubs have eyes on the Premier League.

Who will be Wales' finest?

Wrexham ended last season as top dogs in Wales, with Phil Parkinson's side finishing seventh in the Championship and Vitor Matos' Swansea seven points worse off in 11th.

It was the first time since 2000-01 - when they came 10th in what is now League One - that Wrexham had finished a campaign as the best-placed Welsh side in the English pyramid.

After three successive promotions, Wrexham, who beat Swansea at home in March after losing the reverse fixture last December, narrowly missed out on a play-off chance in May.

But their best-in-Wales status was another sign of the extraordinary progress they have made since Hollywood stars Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac took charge of the club in 2021.

Cardiff City's promotion from League One means that for only the third time, Wales' three heavyweight clubs are together in the second tier this season.

Given that the three teams have never competed together in the top flight - Swansea and Cardiff have met there in just one season, while Wrexham have not played at the highest level - a three-way Championship scrap is a big deal in Wales.

But to an extent the fight to be crowned the nation's leading team is a sideshow, with both Swansea and Wrexham chasing a greater prize.

Most observers would regard Cardiff as outsiders to feature in the promotion race next spring as they look to re-establish themselves at second-tier level.

But the picture is different for Swansea and Wrexham, who both showed considerable ambition in the transfer market for the second year in a row this summer as they look to compete with the Championship's top sides.

These are very early days in the season, but the signs from Swansea have been encouraging, with a tally of 10 points from four games putting them on top of the table.

They have conceded only one league goal so far - the best record in the EFL - while Matos' team produced some of Swansea's best football in years during Tuesday's win over Watford.

The Swans are in buoyant mood, while Wrexham should make the journey south with renewed confidence following their midweek triumph at Millwall.

The Red Dragons endured a concerning start to the season, with chances going begging in their draws with Cardiff and Watford before they were deservedly beaten at home by a Birmingham City team who were under pressure to deliver a result.

But the mood at the Racecourse has lightened significantly thanks to that emphatic victory over a Millwall side who are widely tipped to compete for promotion once more this season.

Another away success this weekend would make this a huge week for Parkinson and his players.

A home win, by contrast, would add to the feeling that Matos' new-look team could end Swansea's run of five successive mid-table Championship finishes by securing a place in the newly extended play-offs.

Big names - and big transfer windows

The fact that Swansea against Wrexham has been selected for a Saturday evening live television slot says something about the interest in the game, which will be watched well beyond Wales' border.

There will be plenty looking on from the United States, for example, given the owners of the two clubs.

In the red corner are Reynolds and Mac, whose Welcome to Wrexham television series has turned what was a non-league football club into a global brand.

And in the white corner are Snoop Dogg, Luka Modric and Martha Stewart, all of whom have become co-owners at Swansea over the past 17 months.

The set-up at each club is different, with Reynolds and Mac the majority owners of Wrexham while Swansea's big names in the boardroom hold only minor stakes.

But the idea at Swansea, whose majority owners are American businessmen Brett Cravatt and Jason Cohen, is to "do a Wrexham" by raising their profile through the non-playing stars associated with the club.

The theory is that increased profile means increased income, which in turn allows more money to be spent on strengthening the team.

At this stage, it is difficult to judge what difference Snoop and Co have made.

But what is not in question is that for a second successive year, Swansea showed significant ambition in the transfer market.

Eight years after a golden period in their history ended with relegation from the Premier League, Swansea look like a club determined to have a serious go at getting back to the highest level.

For Wrexham, the goal is to join the elite for the first time, with their intent even more apparent based on the head-turning sums they have spent on transfers since promotion to the Championship in 2025.

We wait to discover whether either club has sufficient resources to mount a genuine push for the Premier League this season.

And while nothing will be decided in early September, there may be a few clues on offer this weekend.
